teaching_brief.paper: Paper 3 (Area of Study 3): Philosophy and Ethics. 50 minutes, 51 marks, 25% of the qualification. Two questions, each lettered (a) to (d). SPaG and specialist terminology carry a minimum of 5% of the marks on this paper.
teaching_brief.house_question_pattern: Every lesson carries exactly six questions built from the four registered tariffs: two 3-mark Outline Three, one 4-mark Explain Two, two 5-mark Explain Two with Sources, one 12-mark Evaluate a Statement. Mark schemes are written in the band style already used across this subject (Top band (10-12) / Upper-mid band (7-9) / Lower-mid band (4-6) / Low band (1-3) for the 12-mark question; per-point credit for the shorter ones). Never write exam-board Level descriptors.
spec_requirements_every_lesson: DIVERGENT views inside the tradition are compulsory. For Christianity that means Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant (Anglican and nonconformist/evangelical) traditions named separately with their own sources. For Islam it means Sunni and Shi'a, and where relevant reformist and traditionalist scholarship.
NON-RELIGIOUS views (atheist and Humanist) are compulsory, and the specification names situation ethics as an ethical theory to apply to family planning and to divorce.
Every doctrinal claim must be anchored to the source the specification names for that bullet.
common_misconceptions: Treating Catholic teaching as though it were all of Christianity. On the Christianity route (3B) the Catholic position is ONE named strand among Orthodox, Anglican and other Protestant positions, not the default.
Treating Muslim teaching as monolithic. Contraception, divorce procedure and gender roles all carry genuine Sunni/Shi'a and traditionalist/reformist divergence.
Assuming all Christians reject artificial contraception. Most Protestant Churches, and the Anglican Communion since the 1930 Lambeth Conference, permit it.
Assuming Islam forbids contraception outright. The hadith on 'azl (coitus interruptus) are the classical basis for permitting reversible family planning by mutual consent.
Confusing divorce with annulment, and confusing a Muslim divorce pronouncement with the waiting period ('iddah) that follows it.
Reading 'equality' as 'identical roles'. Both traditions contain complementarian and egalitarian readings, and students must be able to state both.
writing_rules: The per-lesson must_cover list is a TEACHING AGENDA, not a verified source. Where it names a date, a document, a decision of a church body or a procedural detail, use it only if you are certain of it; if you are not certain, describe the position without the date or the number. An unverifiable date is worse than no date.
Describe what believers hold without editorialising. Present contested positions as believers hold them.
Do not name a specific verse unless the wording and the reference are both certain; paraphrase the doctrinal point instead.

Do not invent papal, episcopal or scholarly quotations. Where a document is named (for example Humanae Vitae, the Catechism, a Lambeth Conference resolution) describe its teaching rather than quoting it, unless the wording is certain.

article_units.name: Paper 3: Philosophy and Ethics (Islam)
article_units.subtitle: Arguments for the existence of Allah and Muslim teaching on relationships and families

lessons.title: Contraception, Divorce, Gender Equality and Discrimination
lessons.description: Muslim teaching on contraception, divorce, the equality of men and women, and gender discrimination.
lessons.route: ISLAM (Area of Study 3C). Every teaching in this lesson is MUSLIM teaching. There must be no Christian, Catholic or church content of any kind — no Catechism, no Humanae Vitae, no papal teaching, no biblical citation. Sources are the Qur'an and hadith. Divergence means Sunni and Shi'a, and traditionalist versus reformist Muslim scholarship.
section_markers: 2.5 Muslim teaching on contraception: divergent Muslim teachings and attitudes about contraception and family planning, including reference to Sahih al-Bukhari 34:432, and 62:136; different non-religious (including atheist and Humanist) attitudes to family planning and the application of ethical theories, such as situation ethics, and Muslim responses to them.

2.6 Muslim teaching about divorce: divergent Muslim beliefs, teachings and attitudes towards divorce and remarriage, including Surah 2:226-241 and the different rules for performing a divorce in Shi'a and Sunni Islam; different non-religious (including atheist and Humanist) attitudes to divorce and remarriage, including the application of ethical theories, such as situation ethics, and Muslim responses to them.

2.7 Muslim teaching about the equality of men and women in the family: divergent Muslim beliefs, teachings and attitudes about the role of men and women in the family with reference to the Qur'an, including Surah 4 and the time of Muhammad.
2.8 Muslim teachings about gender prejudice and discrimination: Muslim attitudes to gender prejudice and discrimination, including Surah 33:35; examples of gender equality in action in Islam.
must_cover: Contraception: the classical hadith basis for permitting reversible family planning ('azl, withdrawal, reported in Sahih al-Bukhari 34:432 and 62:136); the requirement of mutual consent; the mainstream position that permanent sterilisation and abortion as contraception are treated far more restrictively; the minority position that family planning conflicts with tawakkul (trust in Allah) and with the duty to grow the ummah; non-religious and Humanist family-planning attitudes and situation ethics; Muslim responses.

Divorce: divorce permitted but strongly discouraged; talaq and the waiting period ('iddah) in Surah 2:226-241; khul' as the wife-initiated route; the Sunni and Shi'a procedural difference (Shi'a law requires the pronouncement in Arabic before two just male witnesses in a single sitting and does not recognise triple talaq in one sitting; several Sunni schools have historically treated a triple pronouncement as binding); remarriage permitted; non-religious and Humanist views and situation ethics; Muslim responses.

Equality of men and women in the family: Surah 4 on rights and responsibilities; the mahr and a wife's independent property rights; complementarian readings (qiwamah, maintenance duty) set against egalitarian and reformist readings; the position of women at the time of Muhammad, including Khadijah as a merchant and the reform of inheritance and consent.

Gender prejudice and discrimination: Surah 33:35 addressing believing men and believing women in identical terms; examples of gender equality in action in Muslim communities today; divergent practice on mosque space, scholarship and leadership.

article_units.name: Paper 3: Philosophy and Ethics (Christianity)
article_units.subtitle: Arguments for the existence of God and Christian teaching on relationships and families

lessons.title: Marriage, Sexual Relationships and Family
lessons.description: Christian teaching on marriage, sexual relationships, family life, and the support of the local parish.
lessons.route: CHRISTIANITY (Area of Study 3B) — the BROAD Christian route, NOT the Catholic route. Catholic teaching is one named strand among several and must never dominate. Anglican, nonconformist and evangelical Protestant, and Orthodox positions must each be named with their own sources. There is a separate Catholic route on this platform, so a lesson that reads as Catholic teaching is wrong for this unit.
section_markers: 2.1 The importance and purpose of marriage for Christians: Christian teachings about the significance of marriage in Christian life; the purpose of marriage for Christians, including Mark 10:6-9; divergent Christian and non-religious (including atheist and Humanist) attitudes to the importance of marriage in society, including the sanctity of marriage, a lack of importance, cohabitation and Christian responses to these attitudes.

2.2 Christian teachings about the nature and importance of sexual relationships: divergent Christian teachings about sexual relationships; Christian attitudes towards sexual relationships outside of marriage and same-sex sexual relationships, including interpretations of 1 Corinthians 6:7-20; divergent Christian and non-religious (including atheist and Humanist) attitudes to sexual relationships, including the acceptance of sexual relationships outside marriage and same-sex sexual relationships and Christian responses to them.

2.3 Christian teachings about the purpose and importance of the family: procreation, security and education of children, with reference to Ephesians 6:1-4; divergent Christian responses to different types of family within 21st-century society (nuclear, single parent, same-sex parents, extended and blended families).

2.4 Support for the family in the local parish: how and why the local church community tries to support families, through family worship (including Matthew 19:13-14), rites of passage, classes for parents, counselling and groups for children (including Sunday schools); the importance of the support of the local parish for Christians today.
must_cover: Marriage: Mark 10:6-9 as the named source; marriage as a covenant before God; the Church of England marriage service vows and the Anglican understanding of marriage as a gift of God in creation; the Orthodox crowning ceremony; the Catholic understanding of marriage as one of the seven sacraments; nonconformist and evangelical emphasis on covenant and public promise; Quaker marriage without a priest; divergent Christian and Humanist views on cohabitation and on whether marriage matters in society; Christian responses.

Sexual relationships: 1 Corinthians 6:7-20 and the body as a temple of the Holy Spirit; the traditional teaching that sex belongs within marriage; divergent Christian attitudes to sex before marriage across denominations; same-sex sexual relationships — the Catholic and Orthodox positions, the Church of England's position and its Prayers of Love and Faith, the Methodist Church's 2021 decision to allow same-sex marriages, the Quaker position, and conservative evangelical opposition; Humanist and atheist attitudes; Christian responses.

Family: Ephesians 6:1-4 on children obeying parents and parents not provoking them; procreation, security and education of children; divergent Christian responses to nuclear, single-parent, same-sex-parent, extended and blended families.

Support in the local parish: family worship including Matthew 19:13-14; rites of passage (baptism/dedication, confirmation, marriage, funerals); Sunday schools and youth groups; marriage preparation and counselling; food banks and practical help; why this support matters to Christians today.

lessons.title: Contraception, Divorce, Gender Equality and Discrimination
lessons.description: Christian teaching on contraception, divorce, the equality of men and women, and gender discrimination.
lessons.route: CHRISTIANITY (Area of Study 3B) — the BROAD Christian route, NOT the Catholic route. Catholic teaching is one named strand among several and must never dominate. Anglican, nonconformist and evangelical Protestant, and Orthodox positions must each be named with their own sources. There is a separate Catholic route on this platform, so a lesson that reads as Catholic teaching is wrong for this unit.
section_markers: 2.5 Christian teaching about family planning and regulation of births: divergent Christian attitudes about contraception and family planning, including teachings about the artificial methods of contraception by some Protestant Churches and the Catholic Church, with reference to Humanae Vitae; different non-religious (including atheist and Humanist) attitudes to family planning and the application of ethical theories, such as situation ethics, and Christian responses to them.

2.6 Christian teachings and attitudes towards divorce and remarriage: Christian teachings about divorce and remarriage, including Matthew 19:1-12; divergent Christian, non-religious (including atheist and Humanist) attitudes to divorce and remarriage, including the application of ethical theories, such as situation ethics, and Christian responses to them.

2.7 Christian teaching about the equality of men and women in the family: Christian teachings and attitudes about the role of men and women in the family, including reference to Genesis 1-3 and Ephesians 5:21-30; divergent Christian attitudes about the equality and role of men and women in the family and Christian responses to them.

2.8 Christian teachings about gender prejudice and discrimination: Christian opposition to gender prejudice and discrimination, including Galatians 3:23-29; examples of Christian opposition to gender prejudice and discrimination; divergent Christian attitudes to gender differences, including the role of women in the Church, prejudice and discrimination and Christian responses to them.
must_cover: Contraception: the Anglican shift at the 1930 Lambeth Conference and the general Protestant acceptance of artificial contraception as a responsible exercise of conscience; the Catholic teaching in Humanae Vitae (1968) rejecting artificial contraception while permitting natural family planning, and the unitive-and-procreative reasoning behind it; Orthodox positions; non-religious and Humanist family-planning attitudes; situation ethics applied to family planning; Christian responses.

Divorce and remarriage: Matthew 19:1-12 as the named source and the exception clause; the Catholic teaching that a valid consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, and the difference between annulment and divorce; the Church of England allowing remarriage in church at the minister's discretion since 2002; Orthodox permission for a second and third marriage with a penitential rite (oikonomia); free-church and evangelical variety; non-religious and Humanist attitudes; situation ethics applied to divorce; Christian responses.

Equality of men and women in the family: Genesis 1-3 read both as equal creation in the image of God and, on other readings, as an order of headship; Ephesians 5:21-30 on mutual submission and on husbands loving their wives as Christ loved the Church; complementarian versus egalitarian Christian readings; Christian responses.

Gender prejudice and discrimination: Galatians 3:23-29 (there is neither male nor female, for all are one in Christ Jesus); the ordination of women — the Church of England ordaining women as priests from 1994 and consecrating women as bishops from 2015, the Methodist and United Reformed practice, and the Catholic and Orthodox reservation of ordination to men; examples of Christian opposition to gender discrimination; divergent Christian attitudes; Christian responses.
